Yes, there is evidence suggesting that schizophrenia patients with high intelligence may have a clinically distinct subtype. Research has found that individuals with high intellectual ability (i.e., high IQ) are more likely to experience fewer negative symptoms compared to those with typical schizophrenia.

Studies have identified genetic variants associated with higher IQ and schizophrenia, which may contribute to this disparity in symptom expression. These findings support the idea of a psychosis spectrum or continuum over boundaried diagnostic categories, where individuals with different levels of intellectual ability can be distinguished from each other based on their symptoms and responses to treatment.

While more research is needed to fully understand these findings, the existing evidence suggests that high-intelligence schizophrenia patients may require tailored approaches in diagnosis, treatment, and support. This could involve personalized assessments, specialized therapies, and increased attention to lifestyle factors that impact brain health and functioning.

It's essential to note that this specific subtype of schizophrenia should not be pathologized or stigmatized, as individuals with high intelligence and a clinically distinct subtype are still vulnerable to the same risks and challenges associated with the disorder.
